blurb: Structural systems from cast-in-place concrete to mass timber, off-site modular and panelized building, on-site robots and 3D-printed concrete, low-carbon cement, BIM and delivery models — compared on where the work happens, what it actually changes, and how much capital it takes to start.
question: What actually gets built faster or cheaper, and where does the saving come from?
title: Construction Technology: A Practical Reference
lede: Construction is one of the few large industries whose measured productivity has barely moved in fifty years, and most attempts to fix it have failed on the same two things: the work is a one-off project, and the money is spent before anyone knows whether it worked. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} methods and systems across seven classes, with where the work happens, what each one actually changes, and what it takes in capital before the first unit ships.

facets.label: Where the work is
facets.tip: The single biggest structural difference in construction. Factory work is repeatable, weather-independent, and can be inspected once for a whole run, but it needs volume to fill a plant · On site absorbs variation for free and pays for it in productivity · Both means the method splits the work · Design phase means it happens before anyone breaks ground, which is where the cheapest changes are made.

facets.label: Building type
facets.tip: Where the method is used. This matters more than it looks: repetitive multifamily and hotel work is where off-site manufacturing has succeeded, one-off commercial is where it usually has not, and infrastructure runs on entirely different procurement.

facets.label: What it changes
facets.tip: The claim being made. Ask which of these a vendor is actually selling, because the trade is usually explicit: modular buys schedule and pays in capital, low-carbon cement buys emissions and pays in cost, and site robots buy labor hours and pay in mobilization. A method claiming all five is worth a second look.

facets.label: Capital to start
facets.tip: What it takes before the first job. Low means tools and training a subcontractor can buy · Medium means equipment on the order of a piece of plant · High means a factory, and a factory needs a pipeline of work to fill it, which is what has bankrupted most modular builders rather than any failure of the buildings themselves.

facets.label: Maturity
facets.tip: Standard = ordinary practice, priced in every estimate · Growing = proven and spreading, with code and insurance mostly settled · Early = real projects built, still unusual and still carrying a novelty premium · Research = demonstrations only.
